note: Family and Syariah. Anchored on the Constitution and named statutes only. Where a proposition is doctrine rather than text it says so, and no case is cited — see docs/STYLE.md, 'Never invent a citation'.

cards.front: Which statute governs marriage and divorce for non-Muslims in Malaysia?
cards.back: The Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976. It is federal, so the rules are the same in every State.

cards.front: Which court dissolves a non-Muslim marriage?
cards.back: The civil High Court, under the 1976 Act. A Syariah court has no power over it.

cards.front: Does a couple choose whether the civil or the Syariah system applies to their marriage?
cards.back: No. The applicable system is fixed by religion, not by election, and the courts cannot take each other's work.
cards.source: Structure of the dual system under the Federal Constitution.

cards.front: A question begins "a Muslim couple in Kelantan want a divorce". What must you establish before anything else?
cards.back: Which State's enactment applies. Islamic family law is State law, so there is no single Malaysian text to reason from.
cards.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule, State List.

cards.front: Do the Federal Territories have their own Islamic family law?
cards.back: Yes, but it is made by Parliament rather than by a State legislature, because the Federal Territories have no State legislature of their own.
cards.source: Federal Constitution, division of legislative power.

cards.front: One spouse in a civil marriage converts to Islam. What is the first issue?
cards.back: Jurisdiction — which court may dissolve the marriage and decide about the children. The merits come second.

cards.front: Can a court take jurisdiction because no other court will hear an urgent family matter?
cards.back: No. Jurisdiction is conferred by law, not assumed from need. That is what makes conversion cases hard rather than merely unfortunate.

cards.front: Which part of the Constitution allocates power over Islamic law?
cards.back: The Ninth Schedule. Islamic law and the constitution and organisation of Syariah courts sit on the State List.
cards.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule, State List.

cards.front: What are the two limits on Syariah court jurisdiction?
cards.back: Person and subject. It reaches only persons professing Islam, and only matters on the State List. Both must be satisfied.
cards.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule, State List.

cards.front: What does Article 121(1A) of the Federal Constitution provide?
cards.back: That the civil High Courts have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.

cards.front: Does Article 121(1A) make the Syariah courts superior to the civil courts?
cards.back: No. It removes civil jurisdiction where a matter is within Syariah jurisdiction. It creates no hierarchy and extends no Syariah power.

cards.front: Two Muslims dispute a commercial debt. Which court, and why?
cards.back: The civil courts. The persons are within Syariah reach but the subject is contract, a federal matter, so the second limit fails.

cards.front: Why does the answer to a Syariah jurisdiction question always begin by naming a State?
cards.back: Because each State legislates its own Islamic law and its own courts. There is no single national Syariah statute to reason from.
cards.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule, State List.

cards.front: Are the punishments a Syariah court may impose unlimited?
cards.back: No. Parliament has legislated a ceiling. A State enactment going beyond it exceeds the power the Constitution gives the State.
cards.source: Federal legislation limiting Syariah court punishments.

cards.front: A State enactment exceeds the federal ceiling on Syariah punishments. What kind of argument attacks it?
cards.back: Legislative competence — the same shape used against any State law exceeding the State List. It is about who may legislate, not about religion.
cards.source: Federal Constitution, division of legislative power.
